name: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised (M-CHAT-R/F)

citation.title: Validation of the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-up (M-CHAT-R/F)
citation.authors: Robins, D. L., Casagrande, K., Barton, M., Chen, C. M., Dumont-Mathieu, T., & Fein, D.
citation.copyrightNotice: © 2009 Diana Robins, Deborah Fein, & Marianne Barton. Used for clinical/informational screening.
citation.clinicalDisclaimer: SCREENING TOOL ONLY: This instrument is an initial developmental screener, NOT a diagnostic assessment. A positive screening score does not confirm an autism spectrum condition, and a negative score does not rule out developmental concerns. Always discuss results with a qualified pediatrician or developmental pediatrician.

riskThresholds.label: Low likelihood of needing further evaluation
riskThresholds.summary: Your responses indicate typical developmental progress in social communication milestones.
recommendedActions: If your child is under 24 months, screen again after their second birthday as developmental patterns continue to evolve.
Continue tracking milestones using our developmental checklist.
Share any observations or parental intuition with your pediatrician at your next well-child visit.

riskThresholds.label: Medium likelihood of needing further evaluation
riskThresholds.summary: Your responses indicate some developmental milestones may benefit from clinical follow-up.
recommendedActions: Schedule an appointment with your pediatrician or developmental specialist for a structured follow-up interview.
Download and take the PDF report generated by this screening to your doctor's visit.
Observe your child's responses to name calls and pointing in various calm home settings.

riskThresholds.label: High likelihood of needing further evaluation
riskThresholds.summary: Your responses highlight key areas in social communication and sensory processing that warrant prompt professional evaluation.
recommendedActions: Seek a prompt referral to a pediatric neurologist, developmental pediatrician, or child psychologist.
Early intervention services can begin even before formal diagnosis; early support offers significant benefits.
Take this comprehensive screening report to your clinical consultation.

questions.text: If you point at something across the room, does your child look at it?
questions.exampleText: For example, if you point at a toy or an animal across the room, does your child look in that direction?

questions.text: Have you ever wondered if your child might be deaf?
questions.exampleText: For example, do they often fail to react to loud noises or voice calls even when nearby?

questions.text: Does your child play pretend or make-believe?
questions.exampleText: For example, pretend to drink from an empty cup, talk on a toy phone, or feed a doll or stuffed animal?

questions.text: Does your child like climbing on things?
questions.exampleText: For example, climbing furniture, playground equipment, or stairs?

questions.text: Does your child make unusual finger movements near his or her eyes?
questions.exampleText: For example, does your child wiggle or flap fingers close to their eyes for prolonged periods?

questions.text: Does your child point with one finger to ask for something or to get help?
questions.exampleText: For example, pointing to a snack or toy that is out of reach?

questions.text: Does your child point with one finger to show you something interesting?
questions.exampleText: For example, pointing to an airplane in the sky or a big truck on the road to share the excitement?

questions.text: Is your child interested in other children?
questions.exampleText: For example, does your child watch other children, smile at them, or try to go up to them?

questions.text: Does your child show you things by bringing them to you or holding them up for you to see?
questions.exampleText: Not just to get help, but simply to share experience (e.g. showing you a flower or picture)?

questions.text: Does your child respond when you call his or her name?
questions.exampleText: For example, does your child look up, turn toward you, or make a sound when you call their name?

questions.text: When you smile at your child, does he or she smile back at you?
questions.exampleText: Warm social smiling in response to your smile or warm facial expression.

questions.text: Does your child get upset by everyday noises?
questions.exampleText: For example, does your child scream or cry at noises like a vacuum cleaner, blender, or hairdryer?

questions.text: Does your child walk?
questions.exampleText: Walking independently without assistance across the room.

questions.text: Does your child look you in the eye when you are talking to him or her, playing, or dressing?
questions.exampleText: Comfortable, natural eye contact during typical day-to-day engagement.

questions.text: Does your child try to copy what you do?
questions.exampleText: For example, wave bye-bye, clap hands, or make a funny face when you do it?

questions.text: If you turn your head to look at something, does your child look around to see what you are looking at?
questions.exampleText: Following your gaze to see what caught your attention.

questions.text: Does your child try to get you to watch him or her?
questions.exampleText: For example, does your child say 'Look' or make eye contact to see if you are watching their play?

questions.text: Does your child understand when you tell him or her to do something?
questions.exampleText: For example, without you pointing, do they understand 'Put the book on the table' or 'Bring me your shoe'?

questions.text: If something new happens, does your child look at your face to see how you feel about it?
questions.exampleText: For example, if they hear a strange noise, do they look at your face to see if you are calm or worried?

questions.text: Does your child like movement activities?
questions.exampleText: For example, being swung, bounced on your knees, or gently tossed in play?
